## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

{{< include ../learning_objectives/0650-containers-docker-compose.qmd >}}

## Docker Compose to launch containers

It can be fiddly and error-prone to type long commands into the terminal,
or a GUI every time you want to launch a container.
Even if you are copying and pasting commands,
it can be difficult to make changes to long commands because you cannot click
to a location to make edits.

A better approach is to use Docker Compose to specify how you want
to launch the container.
This way, all the parts of your command are saved in a file.
This helps document how to run the Docker image,
and it can be version controlled as part of a project.

Docker Compose uses a YAML file, specifically named `docker-compose.yml`,
to record how the container should be launched.
This file can include details such as:

- the Docker image and version to use, or how to build it
- how to mount volumes
- what ports to map
- what environment variables to set

`docker run` commands are interchangeable with the parameters specified
in `docker-compose.yml`;
the compose file makes it easier to manage all the `docker run` parameters.
See this resource that can convert a run command to a compose file:
<https://www.composerize.com/>

Here is the `docker-compose.yml` file of [docker-uv-renv](https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv),
the project from [Python and R in one image](0648-containers-uv-renv.qmd):

```{.yaml}
services:
  ## the service name, as in docker compose run analysis-env
  analysis-env:
    ## docker compose build: builds from this folder's Dockerfile and names it with image:.
    ## docker compose up: downloads image: first, and builds only if it can't
    build: .

    ## from Docker Hub; the publish workflow writes the sha- tag here.
    ## Use a sha- tag, not latest: Docker reuses your old copy of latest.
    # image: chendaniely/docker-uv-renv:sha-1a2b3c4

    ## built on your computer only
    image: docker-uv-renv

    ## Uncomment the next two lines if your Dockerfile has no CMD,
    ## or its CMD opens a prompt, such as CMD ["bash"].
    ## (With no CMD, the FROM image's default runs: bash on ubuntu, R on rocker.)
    ## A prompt exits at once without a terminal, so the container would stop
    ## right after `docker compose up --detach`.
    ## Not needed here: the Dockerfile's sshd CMD keeps the container running.
    # stdin_open: true  ## docker run -i
    # tty: true         ## docker run -t

    ports:
      ## 2222 on your computer, 22 in the container.
      ## "127.0.0.1:2222:22" stops others on the same Wi-Fi from reaching it.
      - "2222:22"

    volumes:
      - .:/workspace
      ## ro: read-only
      - ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub:/root/.ssh/authorized_keys:ro
```

Without Docker Compose, building the image and starting the container
takes these two commands, from the project folder:

```bash
docker build --tag docker-uv-renv .
docker run --detach -p 2222:22 -v "$(pwd):/workspace" -v ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub:/root/.ssh/authorized_keys:ro docker-uv-renv
```

Each part of the `docker run` command is a line of the file:

- `services:` lists the containers the project runs.
  This project has one, which it calls `analysis-env`.
- `build: .` builds the image from the `Dockerfile` in this folder,
  like `docker build .`.
- `image: docker-uv-renv` names the image, like `--tag docker-uv-renv`.
- `ports:` maps port 2222 on your computer to port 22 in the container,
  like `-p 2222:22`.
  Port 22 is where the container's ssh server listens.
  The file uses 2222 on your computer, because your computer may already use 22.
- `volumes:` mounts two things, like the two `-v` options.
  `.:/workspace` mounts the project folder at `/workspace`.
  The second line mounts your ssh public key as the list of keys
  that may log in to the container as `root`,
  and `ro` makes it read-only inside the container.
  The key is the one from [SSH for authentication](0210-ssh-authentication.qmd).
- The lines that start with a single `#` are switched off.
  The `image:` line with a Docker Hub name downloads a published image instead of building it
  (see [Publish the image](https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv#publish-the-image)
  in the project's README).
  A service has only one image,
  so to use it, switch it on and switch off the `image: docker-uv-renv` line.
  The `stdin_open:` and `tty:` lines are for images without a `CMD` that keeps running,
  which the callout "Service not running?" below explains.

::: {.callout-note title="No ssh key yet?"}
To check that you have the key, list it:

```bash
ls ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
```

If `ls` says `No such file or directory`,
make a key as in [SSH for authentication](0210-ssh-authentication.qmd):

```bash
ssh-keygen -t ed25519
```

Press Enter to save it in the default place, `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`.
Make the key before you start the container.
If the key is missing when the container starts,
Docker makes a folder at `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub` instead,
and you cannot log in to the container.
:::

Docker Compose reads the paths in the file itself,
so the same file works on macOS, Linux and Windows,
without the Git Bash `/$(pwd)` change from the earlier chapters.

## Docker Compose commands

Run these from the project folder.
`docker compose build` builds the image.
If you built it in [Python and R in one image](0648-containers-uv-renv.qmd),
Docker reuses every layer:

```bash
docker compose build
```

`docker compose up --detach` starts the container.
`--detach` runs it in the background,
so that you get your terminal back while the ssh server keeps running:

```bash
docker compose up --detach
```

```out
[+] up 2/2
 ✔ Network docker-uv-renv_default          Created                                              0.0s
 ✔ Container docker-uv-renv-analysis-env-1 Started                                              0.2s
```

`docker compose up --detach --build` does both steps in one command.
It builds the image first, then starts the container.

Docker Compose made a network for the project's containers,
and named the container after the project folder and the service.
`docker compose ps` lists the project's running containers:

```bash
docker compose ps
```

```out
NAME                            IMAGE            COMMAND               SERVICE        CREATED        STATUS                  PORTS
docker-uv-renv-analysis-env-1   docker-uv-renv   "/usr/sbin/sshd -D"   analysis-env   1 second ago   Up Less than a second   0.0.0.0:2222->22/tcp, [::]:2222->22/tcp
```

`docker compose exec` runs a command in the running container.
Give it the service name from `docker-compose.yml`, `analysis-env`,
and then the command.
This runs a line of Python with the project's Python packages:

```bash
docker compose exec analysis-env uv run python -c "print('hello')"
```

```out
hello
```

To run a script,
make a file called `hello.py` in the project folder on your computer,
in your editor,
with this one line:

```{.python filename="hello.py"}
print("hello")
```

Then run it in the container:

```bash
docker compose exec analysis-env uv run hello.py
```

```out
hello
```

The container can run the file you just made on your computer,
because the project folder is mounted at `/workspace`.

::: {.callout-note title="Service not running?"}
`docker compose exec` needs the container to be running,
and a container runs only as long as its main command,
the `CMD` in its `Dockerfile`.
This project's `CMD` starts an ssh server, which keeps running.

If you write your own `Dockerfile` without a `CMD`,
for example one that starts `FROM ubuntu:24.04`,
the image's main command is `bash`.
With no terminal attached, `bash` finishes as soon as it starts,
and so does the container.
`docker compose ps` does not list it,
and `docker compose exec` stops with this error:

```out
service "analysis-env" is not running
```

To keep the container running,
give `bash` an open input and a terminal in `docker-compose.yml`,
the Docker Compose versions of `-i` and `-t` in `docker run -it`:

```{.yaml}
services:
  analysis-env:
    build: .
    stdin_open: true  # like -i
    tty: true         # like -t
    volumes:
      - .:/workspace
```
:::

Run `bash` in the container to get a terminal in it, in `/workspace`:

```bash
docker compose exec analysis-env bash
```

Then, at the container's prompt:

```bash
pwd
ls
```

```out
/workspace
DESCRIPTION  Makefile     docker-compose.yml  renv       uv.lock
Dockerfile   README.md    hello.py            renv.lock
LICENSE      _quarto.yml  pyproject.toml      reports
```

`/workspace` shows the project folder, including `hello.py`,
because it is mounted there.
Type `exit` to leave the container, which keeps running.
`docker compose down` stops and removes the container and its network:

```bash
docker compose down
```

```out
[+] down 2/2
 ✔ Container docker-uv-renv-analysis-env-1 Removed                                              0.3s
 ✔ Network docker-uv-renv_default          Removed                                              0.1s
```

`docker compose down` only stops this project's containers.
To stop every running container on your computer,
whichever project started it,
give `docker stop` the IDs of all of them:

```bash
docker stop $(docker ps -q)
```

`docker ps -q` (`--quiet`) lists only the IDs of the running containers,
and `$(...)` puts that list in the `docker stop` command.
If no container is running,
`docker stop` gets no IDs and says that it `requires at least 1 argument`,
which you can ignore.
`docker stop` only stops the containers.
Run `docker compose down` in a project's folder to remove that project's containers.

Here are the steps together:

```bash
# 1. Build the image from the Dockerfile that docker-compose.yml points to
docker compose build

# 2. Start the container in the background
docker compose up --detach

# 3. Run commands in the running container
docker compose exec analysis-env uv run python -c "print('hello')"
docker compose exec analysis-env uv run hello.py
docker compose exec analysis-env bash          # interactive shell

# 4. Stop and remove the container
docker compose down
```

## `docker exec` and `docker compose exec`

A container that Docker Compose starts is an ordinary Docker container,
so `docker exec` can run commands in it too.
To try it, start the container again from the project folder:

```bash
docker compose up --detach
```

`docker exec` needs the container's name instead of the service name.
The `NAME` column of `docker compose ps` shows it,
`docker-uv-renv-analysis-env-1`:

```bash
docker exec docker-uv-renv-analysis-env-1 uv run hello.py
```

```out
hello
```

To get a terminal in the container,
`docker exec` needs `-it`,
like `docker run -it` in [Using and running containers](0620-containers-running.qmd):

```bash
docker exec -it docker-uv-renv-analysis-env-1 bash
```

Without `-it`, `bash` has no input and no terminal,
so it finishes at once and you get your own prompt back, with no error.
`docker compose exec` sets up both for you.

`docker compose exec` finds the container through the `docker-compose.yml` file
in the folder you run it from.
From any other folder, it stops with this error:

```out
no configuration file provided: not found
```

`docker exec` works from any folder,
because the container's name says which container you mean.

This matters when you have several projects.
Docker Compose names each container after its project folder and service,
like `docker-uv-renv-analysis-env-1`,
so two projects can both have a service called `analysis-env`.
`docker compose exec analysis-env` picks the one from the folder you are in,
and with `docker exec` you pick one by its full name.

|                       | `docker exec`                         | `docker compose exec`                      |
|-----------------------|---------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| Which container       | its name, from `docker ps`            | the service name, from `docker-compose.yml` |
| Where you can run it  | any folder                            | the project folder                         |
| Terminal for `bash`   | add `-it`                             | set up for you                             |
| Several projects      | you choose by the full name           | uses the project in the current folder     |

In a Docker Compose project, use `docker compose exec`,
because the service name is short and you do not have to look up the container's name.
Use `docker exec` for a container that Docker Compose did not start,
or when you are not in the project folder.

When you are done, stop the container:

```bash
docker compose down
```

## Running a Docker container non-interactively using the Docker Compose

We can also use Docker Compose to run a command in a new container,
non-interactively.
`docker compose run` starts a new container for a service,
runs the command you give it,
and `--rm` deletes the container when the command finishes.
For example, this renders the project's reports,
like the `docker run` command in [Python and R in one image](0648-containers-uv-renv.qmd),
with the image and the mounts taken from `docker-compose.yml`:

```bash
docker compose run --rm analysis-env uv run quarto render
```
